# Incident Report — MTA 2024-07-30 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Evidence Reviewed
- `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 packets, 585.7 sec capture). No separate IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory — findings below are derived entirely from packet analysis via tshark.

## 1. Infected Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **172.16.1.66** |
| MAC address | **00:1e:64:ec:f3:08** (Intel_ec:f3:08), confirmed via ARP (`172.16.1.66 is at 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08`) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** (NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` records; also `DESKTOP-SKBR25F.wiresharkworkshop.online`) |
| AD domain | wiresharkworkshop.online (DC: WIRESHARK-WS-DC, 172.16.1.4) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **ccollier** (Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString from 172.16.1.66) |
| OS (self-reported by malware) | Microsoft Windows 11 Pro, 64-bit, Windows Defender present |

## 2. Malware Family

**STRRAT** — **signature-confirmed**, not merely behavioral. The malware's own C2 beacon protocol transmits the literal string `STRRAT` plus a version number in every check-in, observed in cleartext TCP (stream 83, frame 9066 onward):

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender|<base64 window title>|1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

- Reported STRRAT version: **1.6**
- Bot/campaign ID: **1BE8292C**
- Active window field decodes from base64 `UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy` → `Program Manager` (idle desktop)
- Beacon fired every ~5 seconds for the entire remainder of the capture: **102 pings observed over 508.7 seconds** (76.99s to end of capture at 585.66s), session still open when capture ended.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control:**
- **141.98.10.79:12132/TCP** — raw TCP, plaintext pipe-delimited STRRAT ping protocol, no TLS. Connection was made by hardcoded IP:port; no DNS query anywhere in the capture resolves to 141.98.10.79, confirming a hardcoded C2 address.

**Domains:**
- No malicious domain resolves to the C2 IP (direct-to-IP C2).
- Delivery-associated (not necessarily malicious themselves — abused legitimate infrastructure) DNS/TLS activity immediately preceding first C2 beacon:
  - `github.com` → 140.82.113.3 (query+TLS session at t≈64.0s)
  - `objects.githubusercontent.com` → 185.199.110.133 (t≈64.8s, ~828 KB downloaded from server to client)
  - `repo1.maven.org` → 199.232.196.209 (t≈64–68s, ~8.87 MB downloaded from server to client, matching a Java-related fetch consistent with STRRAT being Java-based)
  - `javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com` seen later (Java Update check), consistent with a JRE present/being used to run the malware.
  - First STRRAT beacon begins at t=76.99s, ~9–13 seconds after this download activity completes — consistent with this being the infection/loader stage, though the sessions are TLS-encrypted and their content could not be inspected.

**URLs / files / hashes:**
- **None recoverable.** All traffic to github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com, and repo1.maven.org was TLS-encrypted with no key log available, so no filenames, URIs, or SHA256 hashes could be extracted for the payload. The only two cleartext HTTP transactions in the capture are unrelated to the payload:
  - `GET http://www.msftconnecttest.com/connecttest.txt` → 200 "Microsoft Connect Test" (standard Windows NCSI check)
  - `GET http://ip-api.com/json/` (UA: Chrome/73.0.3683.86, an outdated/embedded UA string) → 200 JSON geolocation for the host's public IP, region "Texas", country "United States" — timing (t=77.87s, immediately after the first C2 beacon) and the matching `US:United States` field in the STRRAT ping strongly suggest this lookup was performed by the malware itself, not by user browsing.

## Summary
172.16.1.66 (DESKTOP-SKBR25F, user ccollier, Windows 11 Pro) is actively beaconing to a STRRAT remote-access-trojan C2 at 141.98.10.79:12132 over plaintext TCP, self-identifying as STRRAT v1.6 with bot ID 1BE8292C. The beacon was live and ongoing at the end of the capture. Payload delivery appears to have occurred via GitHub-hosted content and a Maven Central fetch roughly 9–13 seconds before the C2 session started, but that traffic was TLS-encrypted and no file artifact or hash could be recovered from this capture alone.
